issues.detail: The skill is a template plus principles with no step-by-step procedure for how the agent should gather inputs, handle missing evidence, or sequence drafting and review; the process is only implied by the examples.

scenarios.name: prd-for-shared-review-boards
scenarios.rationale: A has an evidence-based problem section (with placeholders), exactly one primary metric with baseline and target, counter-metrics, non-goals, pass/fail checkbox acceptance criteria and open questions, though it includes some implementation dictation; B lacks a single primary metric with baseline and target, has no counter-metrics beyond one guardrail, no acceptance criteria, an unevidenced problem section, and more implementation dictation.

scenarios.name: review-vague-permissions-prd
scenarios.rationale: B gives a section-by-section findings table with a concrete numeric metric example, a testable '<1s for 500 members' replacement, edge cases including the last admin and conflicting roles across teams, and launch/rollback criteria. A covers most of the same ground but never mentions conflicting roles across teams, gives no concrete numeric primary metric, names no go/no-go launch criteria, and runs closer to a generic PRD template.

scenarios.name: prd-for-ai-support-assistant
scenarios.rationale: Both give measurable test-set criteria, fallbacks, and staged rollout with rollback, but B is stronger on the rubric: it names a feature flag explicitly, has an explicit go/no-go launch criteria checklist, and has a clear pass/fail test-set grading protocol (300 tickets, two reviewers, ≥85% correct); A has good eval criteria and rollback triggers but never names a feature flag or gives an explicit go/no-go list (only release gates), and includes some implementation-specific details.
